# Video Generation

Video generation is a *generalization* of image generation: a model samples a clip $\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times 3}$ from $p_\theta(\mathbf{V} \mid \mathbf{c})$, conditioned on a control signal $\mathbf{c}$ — typically a text prompt, but also an image (image-to-video), a previous clip (extension/continuation), or a structured pose/depth/camera trajectory. An image is the degenerate case $T=1$, so anything that works for image generation is a candidate for video — but the temporal axis adds two requirements that dominate the engineering:

1. **Temporal consistency**: independently generated frames flicker — identities drift, lighting jumps, textures re-roll. Modeling joint dependencies across frames is what separates a video model from a slideshow.
2. **Sequence length / memory**: a 5-second 720p clip at 24 fps is $\sim 3.3 \times 10^8$ pixels. Even after an 8×8×4 latent compression, a denoiser operates on $\sim 10^6$ tokens per clip — memory and compute are the dominant constraints, and nearly every video-generation paper since 2022 is a memory trick in some form.

The 2022–2026 landscape splits along two largely independent axes: **what is the denoiser** (U-Net + temporal layers vs. Diffusion Transformer), and **how much video training does the model see** — train from scratch (@sec-gen-scratch), fine-tune a pretrained image model (@sec-gen-finetune), or train-free inference-time adaptation (@sec-gen-trainfree). An orthogonal **autoregressive** line (@sec-gen-ar) tokenizes video and predicts tokens like a language model.

---

## Diffusion Recap and Video-Specific Extensions {#sec-gen-diffusion}

Almost every model in this chapter is a diffusion model following the DDPM forward/reverse process [@ho2020ddpm; @sohl2015deepunsup], accelerated at sampling time by DDIM [@song2021ddim] or faster ODE solvers, and steered by classifier-free guidance [@ho2022classifier] — see Chapter 9 (Diffusion Models) for the full derivation. Three extensions are specific to video:

**3D latent compression**. Running diffusion on raw pixels is infeasible for video. Latent Diffusion Models [@rombach2022ldm] compress $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{z} = \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})$ via a frozen VAE and run diffusion in $\mathbf{z}$-space. For video, the VAE compresses **space and time jointly**: a typical 3D VAE with $8{\times}8{\times}4$ (space $\times$ space $\times$ time) compression reduces a $16 \times 720 \times 1280 \times 3$ clip to a $4 \times 90 \times 160 \times 16$ latent — a 24× memory saving. CogVideoX 1.5 pushes this to $16{\times}16{\times}4$; Sora's 3D VAE is undisclosed but inferred to be similarly aggressive.

**Text conditioning**. Cross-attention from a frozen text encoder remains standard, but the choice of encoder matters: **CLIP-text** (fast, weak on compositional prompts, the Stable Diffusion 1.x/2.x default), **T5-XXL** [@raffel2020t5] (the heavyweight used by Imagen Video, Sora, and CogVideoX — excellent on long/compositional prompts, expensive), and **LLM-as-text-encoder** (hidden states from a Llama-3-class model, used by HunyuanVideo and several 2025 open models — trades T5's robustness for better instruction-following).

**Denoiser architecture: U-Net vs. DiT**. The original image-diffusion denoiser was a U-Net with cross-attention [@ronneberger2015unet; @rombach2022ldm]. Peebles & Xie [@peebles2023dit] showed that a **Diffusion Transformer (DiT)** — a plain transformer over a tokenized latent grid — scales better once data and compute are abundant, for the same reason DiTs win at image generation: parameter sharing across all spatiotemporal positions and direct inheritance of LLM infrastructure (FlashAttention, sequence/pipeline parallelism). The video field followed the same trajectory: 2022–2023 models (VDM, Make-A-Video, Video LDM, SVD) used U-Net + factorized space-time attention or 3D convolutions; 2024 onward (Sora, CogVideoX, Mochi, HunyuanVideo, Wan, LTX-Video) use DiT over a 3D-VAE latent.

---

## Family 1: Training from Scratch on Video {#sec-gen-scratch}

The cleanest baseline — train a denoiser on video data only, with no image pretraining.

### Video Diffusion Models — VDM (2022) {.unnumbered}

VDM [@ho2022vdm] introduced the template: a **3D U-Net factorized over space and time**.

**Spatial processing** (identical to image U-Net): 2D spatial convolutions extended to space-only 3D convolutions (a 3×3 conv becomes 1×3×3); spatial self-attention treats the frame axis as a batch dimension.

**Temporal processing** (new): a **temporal attention block** inserted after each spatial attention block, with spatial axes folded into the batch dimension. The temporal positional embedding is *relative* (no absolute notion of time), enabling generalization to variable-length clips.

**Denoising objective** (same as image DDPM):
$$\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{V}_0, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{V}_t, t)\|^2\right]$$
where $\mathbf{V}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times C}$ is the noised clip at step $t$.

![VDM 3D U-Net factorized over space and time. Spatial attention layers alternate with temporal attention blocks; relative positional embeddings encode frame position.](/images/video/video_diffusion_model.png){#fig-vdm width=80% fig-align="center"}

This factorized design — spatial blocks operating on frames in parallel, temporal blocks acting only across time — became the canonical pattern that almost every 2022–2024 video diffusion model inherits; 2024–2026 DiT variants generalize it with a single transformer attending across $(t,h,w)$ jointly, often with block-sparse masks that recover the factorized form for efficiency.

### Imagen Video (2022, Google) {.unnumbered}

Imagen Video [@ho2022imagenvideo] tackles the *resolution* problem with a **cascade of seven diffusion models** that progressively refine spatial and temporal resolution:

```
Text ──► T5-XXL Encoder ──► Base Model (low-res, few frames)
                                   ↓
              ┌────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
              ▼                    ▼                       ▼
         SSR ×3 (spatial)    TSR ×3 (temporal)      SSR+TSR combined
```

- **Base**: 3D-conv U-Net with spatio-temporal self-attention, conditioned on T5-XXL embeddings; outputs a small, low-res, short clip ($40{\times}24{\times}24$, 16 frames at ~3 fps).
- **SSR** (spatial super-resolution): three stages, $24{\times}24 \to 80{\times}80 \to 240{\times}240 \to 720{\times}720$.
- **TSR** (temporal super-resolution): three stages interpolate $16 \to 32 \to 64 \to 128$ frames (≈5s at 24fps).

**Memory tricks** (critical at scale): replace temporal attention with temporal *convolutions* at high resolution (linear, not quadratic, in frame count), and drop spatial attention entirely at the finest resolution.

![Imagen Video cascade: seven video diffusion models progressively upsample from a low-resolution, short base clip via spatial (SSR) and temporal (TSR) super-resolution stages.](/images/video/imagen.png){#fig-imagen-video width=85% fig-align="center"}

This cascade was the first text-to-video model widely regarded as "production quality" by 2022 standards, and set the template that Sora later inherited.

### Sora (2024, OpenAI) {.unnumbered}

Sora [@openai2024sora] replaces the U-Net with a **DiT**, following the finding that transformers scale better than U-Nets with data and model size. Two architectural breaks:

- **3D spacetime patches**: instead of 2D patches from a single frame, Sora tokenizes the 3D-VAE latent into $p_t \times p_h \times p_w$ spacetime patches (e.g. $2{\times}16{\times}16$), each flattened and linearly projected to a token $\mathbf{z}_i \in \mathbb{R}^D$:
$$\mathbf{z}_i = \mathbf{E} \cdot \text{Flatten}(\mathbf{V}[t_i{:}t_i{+}\Delta t,\; y_i{:}y_i{+}P,\; x_i{:}x_i{+}P])$$
- **Joint spatiotemporal attention**: the transformer applies full self-attention across *all* spacetime tokens, jointly modeling space and time rather than via VDM/Imagen Video's factorized pattern.

$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} = \text{Transformer}_\theta(\{\mathbf{z}_i\}, \text{timestep embedding}, \text{text cross-attention})$$

Text conditioning is standard T5-XXL cross-attention with CFG. The key design insight: tokens from arbitrary-length, arbitrary-resolution videos can all be processed by the same transformer, since attention operates on variable-length sequences — unifying image generation ($T{=}1$) and video generation under one architecture. **Sora 2** (2024) adds synchronized audio generation and improved long-clip coherence.

![Sora: 3D spacetime patch tokenization and DiT-based denoising. Video patches are flattened and projected to tokens; a Transformer applies full self-attention across all spatiotemporal tokens conditioned on text via cross-attention.](/images/video/sora.png){#fig-sora width=85% fig-align="center"}

### CogVideoX / CogVideoX 1.5 (2024, Tsinghua + Zhipu AI) {.unnumbered}

CogVideoX [@yang2024cogvideox] is the canonical **open-weights** train-from-scratch video DiT (5B parameters, Apache-2.0). Three contributions: a 3D-VAE with $4{\times}8{\times}8$ compression ($4{\times}16{\times}16$ in v1.5); **Expert Adaptive LayerNorm**, where conditioning signals (timestep, text) modulate the transformer via dedicated AdaLN "experts" rather than cross-attention — an influential design adopted by many later video DiTs; and disclosed multi-resolution/multi-duration bucketed training, mirroring Sora's inferred recipe.

## Family 2: Fine-Tuning a Pretrained Image Model {#sec-gen-finetune}

The pragmatic majority of 2022–2024 work: start from a strong image diffusion model and *add* temporal layers, often training only those — cheap, and the generator inherits the image model's visual priors and compositional strength.

### Make-A-Video (2022, Meta) {.unnumbered}

Make-A-Video [@singer2022makeavideo] composes three modules: a *pretrained* text-to-image diffusion model, a **frame interpolation network** (increases frame rate), and a **spatiotemporal super-resolution** model.

![Make-a-Video full architecture: a pretrained text-to-image model extended with (2D+1) temporal layers, a frame interpolation network, and a spatiotemporal super-resolution model.](/images/video/make_a_video.png){#fig-make-a-video width=85% fig-align="center"}

New temporal layers inserted into the pretrained model:

- **(2D+1) convolutions**: each 2D spatial conv is followed by a 1D temporal conv initialized to the identity:
$$\text{Conv}_{(2D+1)}(\mathbf{X}) = \text{Conv}_\text{1D-temporal}(\text{Conv}_\text{2D-spatial}(\mathbf{X}))$$
- **(2D+1) attention**: each spatial self-attention layer is followed by a temporal self-attention layer (spatial positions as batch dimension).

![Make-a-Video (2D+1) temporal modules. Each 2D spatial convolution is followed by a 1D temporal convolution (initialized to identity); each spatial attention block is followed by a temporal attention layer.](/images/video/2d1_attention.png){#fig-2d1-attention width=80% fig-align="center"}

Only the new temporal modules are trained; image weights stay frozen, so the model can train jointly on (text, video) and (text, image) pairs — at initialization the temporal layers are identity functions, so the model behaves as the image model on individual frames. The (2D+1) factorization became standard for years.

### Video LDM / Align-Your-Latents (2023) {.unnumbered}

Align-Your-Latents [@blattmann2023videoldm] is the canonical *latent* variant of the same idea, built on a Stable-Diffusion-style LDM:

```
LDM layer (frozen) → Temporal layer (trained) → LDM layer (frozen) → ...
```

Temporal layers (3D convolutions + temporal attention) are interleaved between frozen spatial LDM layers; only temporal parameters are updated. The LDM autoencoder produces flickering when frames are decoded independently, so a video-aware decoder is fine-tuned with:
$$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_\text{recon} + \mathcal{L}_\text{GAN}$$
where $\mathcal{L}_\text{GAN}$ uses a 3D-convolutional discriminator distinguishing real from generated clips.

![Align Your Latents / Video LDM: trainable temporal layers interleaved with frozen spatial LDM layers. Only temporal parameters are updated; spatial parameters stay frozen to preserve image generation quality.](/images/video/align_your_latents.png){#fig-align-your-latents width=85% fig-align="center"}

![Video LDM 3D-convolutional discriminator used to fine-tune the autoencoder decoder with a GAN loss, eliminating per-frame flickering artifacts.](/images/video/discriminator.png){#fig-discriminator width=70% fig-align="center"}

This recipe is the template for **Stable Video Diffusion (SVD)** [@blattmann2023svd] (Stability AI, 2023): the SD-2.1 U-Net plus temporal layers, trained on a curated 5M-clip subset, producing 14- or 25-frame 1024×576 clips. SVD remains the default open-weights *image-to-video* baseline.

---

## Family 3: Training-Free Adaptation {#sec-gen-trainfree}

Inference-time tricks producing video from a pretrained image model with **no weight updates** — cheap and fast, useful as a baseline or for one-off effects, but not competitive on benchmarks.

### Text2Video-Zero (2023) {.unnumbered}

Text2Video-Zero [@khachatryan2023text2videozero] uses two tricks:

**1. Structured latent sampling** (simulates camera motion): sample one noise latent $\mathbf{z}_T$, take a DDIM backward step to get $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_0$, apply translations to $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_0$ (simulating pan/zoom), then a DDPM forward step yields a sequence of noised latents related by a known linear shift:
$$\mathbf{x}_{T'}^1 = \text{DDIM-backward}(\mathbf{x}_T^1, \Delta t), \quad \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{T'}^k = W_k(\mathbf{x}_{T'}^1), \quad \mathbf{x}_T^k = \text{DDIM-forward}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{T'}^k, \Delta t)$$
where $W_k$ applies $(k-1)$ steps of a fixed global motion direction $\boldsymbol{\delta}$.

**2. Cross-frame attention**: reprogram self-attention so each frame's queries attend to the *first* frame's keys/values:
$$\text{Attn}^{(t)} = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}^{(t)} (\mathbf{K}^{(1)})^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)\mathbf{V}^{(1)}$$

![Text2Video-Zero: structured latent sampling simulates camera motion (left); cross-frame attention forces each frame to attend to the keys and values of the first frame, enforcing appearance consistency across frames (right).](/images/video/text2video.png){#fig-text2video-zero width=85% fig-align="center"}

The first frame anchors object identity and background, producing short, coherent video with zero video training. Useful diagnostically: if a frozen image model with these tricks beats a poorly-trained video model with full training, the latter has something wrong.

---

## Autoregressive Video Generation {#sec-gen-ar}

Orthogonal to diffusion: tokenize video into discrete codes and predict the next code, exactly like a language model. A **VQ-VAE** [@vandenoord2017vqvae; @esser2021vqgan] maps a clip to a sequence of integer codes from a fixed codebook (e.g. 16,384 entries); a transformer is trained with next-token-prediction loss on these codes, and sampling decodes codes back to pixels.

**VideoPoet** [@kondratyuk2024videopoet] (Google, 2023) is the first large-scale (~8B-parameter) autoregressive video LM, predicting a unified stream of *image + audio + text* tokens — enabling text-to-video, image-to-video, stylization, and audio-to-video in one model. It uses **MAGVIT-v2** [@yu2024magvit2] as its tokenizer, whose quality improvement was the key enabler for AR video matching diffusion on FVD. **LlamaGen** [@sun2024llamagen] (image-only) is the cleanest demonstration that a vanilla LLaMA transformer with a high-quality VQ tokenizer reaches Stable-Diffusion-level image quality; its tokenizer underlies **Janus-Pro**'s [@chen2025januspro] unified understanding+generation transformer (Chapter 11).

The autoregressive line is attractive for two reasons: it gives a **token-interface unification** with LLMs — one transformer reads and writes both video and text — and it **inherits LLM infrastructure** (speculative decoding, prefix caching, FlashAttention) for free. As of 2026 the diffusion-DiT line remains ahead on raw quality (Sora, Veo 3, CogVideoX 1.5), but AR + diffusion-head hybrids are closing the gap, and **MAGI-1 / Cosmos-1** (NVIDIA) extend the AR line toward world-model generation for robotics.

## Evaluation {#sec-gen-eval}

Video generation evaluation is in a worse state than video understanding evaluation — there is no single "correct" output.

**Distributional metrics**: **Fréchet Video Distance (FVD)** [@unterthiner2018fvd] is the video analogue of FID — compute I3D features for real and generated clips, fit Gaussians, measure 2-Wasserstein distance. Reported on UCF-101/MSR-VTT in nearly every paper despite known sensitivity to clip length, frame rate, and the I3D checkpoint used.

**Compositional metrics**: **VBench / VBench++** [@huang2024vbench] is the dominant 2024–2026 suite, decomposing quality into **16 dimensions** — subject/background consistency, temporal flickering, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic/imaging quality, object class, multiple objects, human action, color, spatial relationship, scene, appearance/temporal style, overall consistency — each scored by a dedicated evaluator (CLIP, ViCLIP, MUSIQ, RAFT). The headline number is a weighted mean, but the per-dimension breakdown is what papers actually argue about. **EvalCrafter** [@liu2024evalcrafter] is a similar ~700-prompt, 17-metric suite often reported alongside VBench.

**Human preference**: side-by-side A/B against a strong baseline (Sora, Veo, CogVideoX-5B) — 50–100 prompts × 3–5 raters, blinded, win rate reported. Almost every 2025–2026 paper includes this because automatic metrics still fail to discriminate among top open models.

**Recommendations for a 2026 paper**: (1) FVD on UCF-101 + MSR-VTT (legacy but expected); (2) VBench full 16 dimensions + headline mean; (3) human-preference A/B against a flagship; (4) a compositional sanity check (T2V-CompBench or a VBench compositional sub-axis) to confirm the model hasn't collapsed to "pretty but wrong."

## Summary: Video Generation Paradigms

| Model | Denoiser | Paradigm | Temporal mechanism | Training data |
|-------|----------|----------|-----------------|--------------|
| VDM | U-Net | Scratch | Temporal attention | Video |
| Imagen Video | U-Net | Scratch (cascade) | 3D conv + spatio-temporal attn | Video |
| Sora / CogVideoX | DiT | Scratch | Full spatiotemporal attention over 3D patches | Video |
| Make-a-Video | U-Net | Fine-tune image model | (2D+1) conv + attn | Video + Images |
| Video LDM / SVD | U-Net | Fine-tune image LDM | 3D conv + temporal attn | Video |
| Text2Video-Zero | U-Net | Training-free | Cross-frame attn (no training) | None |
| VideoPoet | Transformer (AR) | Scratch, token-based | Next-token prediction over VQ codes | Video + Audio + Text |

: Video generation paradigms compared. {#tbl-gen-summary}

**Interview Insight**: The progression VDM → Imagen Video → Sora → CogVideoX traces the same arc as image generation (U-Net → cascades → DiT), but compressed into two years instead of four — because video inherited the image-diffusion playbook wholesale and only had to solve the *temporal* half of the problem.

## Interview Questions

**Q: What is the core architectural difference between Sora/CogVideoX and earlier video diffusion models like VDM or Imagen Video?**

VDM and Imagen Video use a U-Net denoiser with 3D convolutions and *factorized* spatiotemporal attention — spatial and temporal processing are largely separate operations. Sora and CogVideoX replace the U-Net with a **Diffusion Transformer (DiT)**, tokenizing the video into 3D spacetime patches and applying full self-attention jointly across all spatial and temporal positions. This lets the same architecture handle variable-length, variable-resolution video (and degenerate to image generation at $T=1$), and benefits from transformer scaling laws — at the cost of higher per-step compute than the factorized U-Net pattern.

---

**Q: Describe how Make-a-Video generates video without training a video diffusion model from scratch.**

Make-a-Video inserts (2D+1) convolutional and attention layers into a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model: each 2D conv is followed by a temporal 1D conv initialized to the identity, and each spatial attention layer is followed by a temporal attention layer. The image weights stay frozen (or lightly fine-tuned); only the new temporal layers are trained on video data. Because the temporal layers initialize as identity functions, the model initially behaves exactly like the image model on individual frames — a stable starting point that preserves image generation quality while learning motion cheaply.

---

**Q: Why does almost every video generator use a 3D VAE rather than the 2D VAE from image diffusion?**

A 2D VAE compresses each frame independently, so a video tensor is still $T$ times larger than a single image latent — the dominant cost for video diffusion. A 3D VAE compresses space *and* time jointly (e.g. $8{\times}8{\times}4$), giving an additional ~4× reduction along the temporal axis on top of the spatial compression. This is what makes it feasible to run a transformer or U-Net over the latent at all; without it, even a modest 16-frame clip would have a sequence length 16× larger than the equivalent image.

---

**Q: VBench reports 16 separate dimensions instead of one number. Why, and what's the risk?**

Video quality is multi-axis: a model can have excellent per-frame aesthetics but flicker badly (low temporal consistency), or move very little because static frames score well on most metrics (low "dynamic degree"). A single averaged score hides these trade-offs and can be gamed — e.g., a model that barely moves scores well on subject/background consistency. The 16-dimension breakdown lets a paper show *which* axis it improves, but the flip side is that papers increasingly optimize directly for VBench sub-scores rather than for human preference, which is why human A/B testing remains mandatory alongside it.

---

**Q: Compare the autoregressive and diffusion approaches to video generation. Why might unification with LLMs matter beyond raw quality?**

Diffusion generates a clip by iterative denoising of a continuous (or VAE) latent and currently leads on raw visual quality (Sora, Veo 3, CogVideoX 1.5). Autoregressive generation tokenizes video into discrete VQ codes and predicts them one at a time, like text — currently behind on quality but improving rapidly with better tokenizers (MAGVIT-v2). The unification argument is architectural: an AR video model uses the *same* token interface as an LLM, so a single transformer can both understand video (read tokens, write text — Chapter 11) and generate it (read text, write tokens), and inherits every LLM-serving optimization (speculative decoding, KV-cache reuse, prefix sharing) for free. This is why Janus-Pro and the broader "unified" model line bet on AR despite the current quality gap.

---

**Q: How does classifier-free guidance behave differently for video versus image generation?**

CFG blends conditional and unconditional denoiser outputs, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} = \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\varnothing) + w[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\mathbf{c}) - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\varnothing)]$, trading diversity for prompt fidelity. For video, the practical guidance scale is typically higher (6–9 vs. 4–7.5 for images) because the temporal-consistency requirement makes under-conditioned samples noticeably worse — a video that drifts off-prompt over time looks like a different video halfway through, which is far more jarring than a single off-prompt image. Over-guidance also has a video-specific failure mode: oversaturated, low-motion ("frozen") clips, since high guidance pushes toward the conditional mode at the expense of the diversity that produces natural motion.
